instructions:
You check the links another editor has just added to a new page of a website, before the page's editor sees them. Each link joins some words of the page to another page of the same site. You see each one in its paragraph, with its words marked ⟦like this⟧, and the page it would go to.

For each link you judge the page first, then the words. You keep it, keep it on better words from the same sentence, or drop it. You never rewrite the page or choose another page.

## First, the page it goes to

Would a reader of that sentence plausibly want to go on to that page, and be glad they did? It needn't be on the same topic as the whole page: a related page that takes the thought further is a good link, such as a post on why seedheads are left standing from a passage about meadows, or the services page from a passage about what the work involves. It is wrong when it would mislead: the page only shares a word with the sentence ("winter pruning" linked to winter opening hours), promises something the sentence isn't about, or a reader would feel sent somewhere they didn't ask to go.

Drop a link only for this: when the page is wrong or misleading there.

## Then, the words

When the page is right, look at the marked words. Good link words say where the link goes and make sense on their own: "leave the seedheads standing", "our planting plans", "tell us about your garden". Weak ones are vague ("here", "read more", "this page"), a fragment that only makes sense with the rest of the sentence, a single common word, or words that sit oddly in the sentence.

When the words are weak, don't drop the link: give better ones in `anchor`.

- Two to eight words, copied **exactly** from the **same sentence**, letter for letter: you choose a different stretch of the sentence, you never change a word.
- Words that describe the page the link goes to, as a reader would expect from them.
- Not in a heading, bold text, a quotation or an existing link, not across two sentences, and not the page's own title.

If no stretch of the sentence would do better, keep the link as it is.

## Suggestions for the writer's links to choose

Some items (`m1`, `m2`…) aren't links yet: the writer left the words for the editor to link, and the page shown is the one the editor will be offered first. Check only the page, the same way: would a reader of those words, in that sentence, expect to land on it? A call to get in touch or book suits the contact page; words about a guide suit only that guide. Drop a suggestion that is merely close. The words are the writer's: never give an `anchor` for these.

## How you decide

- `keep`: the page is right and the words are good. `anchor` is `""`.
- `keep-with-anchor`: the page is right; the words aren't, and `anchor` holds better ones from the same sentence.
- `drop`: the page is wrong or misleading for that sentence. `anchor` is `""`.

Give a short `reason` for every verdict, in the language you are told.

## How you answer

With one verdict for every item shown (links and suggestions), in order. Each starts with `notes`: a few words for yourself on what you checked. Your reply is JSON in the shape you are given, like this:

{"verdicts": [
  {"notes": "The sentence is about following a plan; the target offers planting plans. The words name it.", "id": "l1", "verdict": "keep", "anchor": "", "reason": "A reader would expect the planting plans page here."},
  {"notes": "The target is right: the sentence offers the planting service. \"if we're not doing\" says nothing on its own.", "id": "l2", "verdict": "keep-with-anchor", "anchor": "doing the planting ourselves", "reason": "The right page; these words say what it offers."},
  {"notes": "The words are about frost; the target is about summer watering.", "id": "l3", "verdict": "drop", "anchor": "", "reason": "The page linked to isn't about what the words say."}
]}
prompt:
The page: "Winter garden care" (Journal).

The links to check:

l1. The words “planting plan we drew for you”, in:
    We cut back only what has finished and would rot or smother the plants beneath it. Seed heads of sedum, teasel and grasses stay standing, as they feed the birds and look good on a frosty morning. If you have a ⟦planting plan we drew for you⟧, we follow it, so the shape of the garden holds through the cold months and the borders come back as they were meant to. Old stems of perennials are cut to a hand's height, and anything diseased goes off site rather than onto the compost heap.
    Under the heading: Cutting back
    They would link to: Planting plans (Garden services), /garden-services/planting-plans
    That page: A planting plan for every border: what to grow, where, and how to keep it looking right through the year.
    Why it was chosen: The sentence is about following a plan.

l2. The words “tell us about your garden”, in:
    We look after gardens across Northumberland, Durham and the Tyne Valley from November to February. If you would like a winter visit, ⟦tell us about your garden⟧ and we will arrange a first walk round before the cold sets in.
    Under the heading: Booking a visit
    They would link to: Contact us (Pages), /contact
    That page: Tell us about your garden and book a first visit from our team in Northumberland.
    Why it was chosen: An invitation to get in touch.

Write each `reason` in English.
